metaDescription: New York to Illinois car shipping to Chicago runs 800 miles in 2 to 3 days for $700 to $800. From Buffalo it is 530 miles and $500 to $600. Neighborhood tips.
h1: New York to Illinois car shipping
heroSub: Chicago is the Midwest's freight hub, which makes this one of the easiest lanes we run. Here is the cost from New York City and from Buffalo, how delivery works in Chicago's neighborhoods, and what winter does to the schedule.
intro:
New York to Illinois car shipping is a short-haul run by our standards. New York City to Chicago is about 800 miles along I-80, and a running sedan on an open carrier typically costs $700 to $800 and arrives 2 to 3 days after pickup. From Buffalo it is closer: roughly 530 miles on I-90, usually 1 to 2 days and $500 to $600. Albany sits at about 830 miles.

Because Chicago is where Midwest loads consolidate, trucks are plentiful in both directions year-round, which keeps the price steady and pickup windows short. The quote tool beside the heading gives a live price; the ranges here are typical for a sedan booked a week out.

sections.h2: Two starting points for New York to Illinois car shipping: I-80 from the city, I-90 from Buffalo
sections.html:
From the Bronx, Long Island and the Hudson Valley, the truck crosses the George Washington Bridge, joins I-80 in New Jersey and stays on it across Pennsylvania, Ohio and Indiana into Chicago. I-80 carries enough car haulers that a Chicago-bound slot opens almost every day. Figure a pickup window of 1 to 3 days and 2 to 3 days on the road.

From our Buffalo office the math is different. I-90 runs along Lake Erie through Cleveland and Toledo and meets I-80 in Indiana, about 530 miles door to door. That is a single driving day, and carriers running Chicago to the Northeast pass through Buffalo anyway, so a Buffalo pickup is often the cheapest per mile we book. Albany and Schenectady cars follow the same road, around 830 miles, at close to the NYC rate.

sections.h2: What New York to Illinois car shipping costs
sections.html:
Expect $700 to $800 for an open carrier from the New York metro to the Chicago area, and $500 to $600 from Buffalo. Enclosed adds 30 to 50 percent, so roughly $950 to $1,150 from the city. SUVs and pickups add $100 to $250, and a car that will not start adds $100 to $200. Downstate destinations such as Champaign, Springfield or Peoria sit off the main truck path and add $50 to $100 plus a day.

This is one of the few lanes where the winter price does not spike, because Northeast to Chicago freight stays heavy all year. August is the busiest month. The car shipping cost guide covers the surcharges, and a three-day flexible pickup window almost always lands at the bottom of the range.

sections.h2: Delivering in Chicago's neighborhoods and the Loop
sections.html:
The North Side neighborhoods are the most common delivery points: Lincoln Park, Lakeview, Wicker Park and Logan Square. They are dense, with alleys and limited street parking, and a 75-foot hauler cannot get down a one-way street with cars parked on both sides. The driver will usually propose a spot a few blocks away: a wide stretch of Ashland or Western, a grocery store lot, or a park. Hyde Park works the same way; University of Chicago students should plan to meet near the Midway.

Downtown in the Loop, River North and Streeterville is a different problem. High-rise garages have low clearances and tight ramps the hauler cannot enter. Lower Wacker Drive is restricted for trucks, and Lake Shore Drive bans them entirely. Most downtown deliveries happen at a surface lot or a wide curb on Columbus or Roosevelt, and you drive the last few blocks yourself.

sections.h2: The suburbs: Evanston, Naperville, Schaumburg, Oak Park and Oak Brook
sections.html:
Suburban Chicago is where most relocation deliveries actually happen, and it is far easier than the city. Evanston is the exception; the streets near Northwestern are narrow and tree-lined, so the driver typically meets students on Sheridan Road or at a lakefront lot. Oak Park's older streets resemble the North Side. Naperville, Schaumburg, Oak Brook and the I-88 and I-90 corporate corridor have wide arterials and office parks built for trucks, so delivery works as described on our door-to-door page.

O'Hare and Midway come up with fly-and-ship customers who hand off the car at a New York office and fly out the same day. We do not deliver to airport lots, but we can time the pickup to a flight and deliver to the home a few days later.

sections.h2: Winter in Chicago: lake-effect snow, salt and cars that will not start
sections.html:
Winter does not change the price much on this lane, but it changes the practical details. Lake-effect snow can shut I-90 near Erie or the Indiana Toll Road for a day at a time, so a 2-day run becomes a 3-day run with no warning; we build that into the estimate from December through March. Illinois and Indiana salt their roads heavily, so wash the underside within a few days of delivery.

The important one: a car that will not start in the cold is inoperable for loading purposes, and if the driver has to winch it onto the deck the carrier is entitled to the $100 to $200 inoperable surcharge on the spot. Charge or replace a weak battery before pickup, run the pre-shipping checklist, and if the car is a known non-runner, say so at booking.

sections.h2: Downstate Illinois, cross-shipping and auction cars coming back to New York
sections.html:
Outside Chicagoland, the regular destinations are Champaign-Urbana for UIUC students, Springfield for state government, Bloomington-Normal for State Farm, Rockford and Peoria. Rockford is easy because trucks pass it heading to Wisconsin; the others sit on I-55, I-57 and I-74 south of the main path, so expect a day longer and a small surcharge. UIUC students should book by late July.

Because Chicago is a hub, many orders cross state lines on one end. A pickup in Hammond, Indiana, or a delivery in Milwaukee rides the same trucks and prices within $50 of Chicago. The lane also runs the other way: New York buyers who win a car at Manheim Chicago, Copart or the Joliet dealer auctions ship it east to the Bronx, Long Island or upstate. Auction cars need a release and a gate pass, and a non-runner needs an inoperable booking.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to ship a car from New York to Chicago?
faqs.a: A running mid-size sedan on an open carrier typically costs $700 to $800 from the New York City metro and $500 to $600 from Buffalo. Enclosed transport adds 30 to 50 percent. SUVs and pickups add $100 to $250, and downstate destinations such as Champaign or Springfield add $50 to $100. Prices hold steady in winter on this lane.

faqs.q: How long does New York to Illinois car shipping take?
faqs.a: From New York City to Chicago, plan on 2 to 3 days of transit after pickup. From Buffalo it is usually 1 to 2 days, since I-90 puts the car in Chicago in a single driving day. Downstate Illinois adds a day, and winter lake-effect snow on I-90 can add another, so we quote a wider window from December through March.

faqs.q: Can the truck deliver to my high-rise downtown?
faqs.a: Not into the garage. Car haulers cannot clear high-rise garage ramps, trucks are restricted on Lower Wacker and banned from Lake Shore Drive, so the driver meets you at a surface lot or a wide curb nearby, often on Roosevelt or Columbus, and you drive the last few blocks. Give us the building address at booking and we set the meeting point in advance.

faqs.q: What if my car will not start in the cold on pickup day?
faqs.a: The carrier treats it as inoperable and winches it aboard, which carries a $100 to $200 surcharge paid on the spot and can push the driver's schedule. Test the battery before a winter pickup and replace it if it is weak. If the car is a known non-runner, tell us when you book so a truck with a winch is dispatched.

faqs.q: Can you ship a car I bought at a Chicago auction to New York?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is a regular part of this lane. We need the auction release or gate pass, the lot number and the yard's pickup hours, and we need to know whether the car runs. Manheim Chicago, Copart and the Joliet dealer auctions all have standard release procedures. Transit east to the Bronx, Long Island or upstate is the same 2 to 3 days.
